newsitem.title: USA: Senator wants new negotiations with Swiss on Nazis.
newsitem.headline: Senator wants new negotiations with Swiss on Nazis.

text.p: Charging that Switzerland grossly deceived the United States on the amount of Nazi assets it held, the head of the U.S. Senate Banking Committee asked the State Department on Tuesday to reopen negotiations with the Swiss on a 50-year-old treaty.

New York Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato's move came as a newly discovered document in the U.S. National Archives claimed Nazi Germany not only had hundreds of millions of dollars in gold secreted in Switzerland at the end of the Second World War, but an even larger amount in other assets that included bank deposits, securities, real estate and looted art works.

The May 31, 1945, document from the American legation in Bern to the secretary of state paints a sweeping picture of German investment in Switzerland but warns that the full truth may never be known because "The traditional stock-in-trade of Swiss bankers, notaries, realtors, insurance companies, attorneys, etc. is the concealment of assets."

The document, obtained by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) during a search of the archives, indicates that the amount in assets -- an estimated $750 million in 1945 dollars -- was greater than what the Nazis had deposited in gold in Switzerland. Other previously secret documents estimated the gold to be worth $550 million in 1945 dollars or about $6 billion today.
In 1946, after freezing Swiss assets in the United States, the United States, Britain and France reached an agreement with Switzerland to return Nazi gold and assets kept in Switzerland.

Under the agreement, the three countries received $60 million in gold and was supposed to get 50 percent of the non-gold assets, an amount that worked out to $121 million over the course of seven years, according to historians. The Swiss were allowed to keep the other 50 percent of assets.
This is the agreement that D'Amato said he wanted renegotiated.
In a letter to Secretary of State Warren Christopher, D'Amato accused Switzerland of 50 years of deception over the amount of funds deposited in Swiss banks by the Nazis.

He said, "When the allies sat down with the Swiss in 1945, in an attempt to gain possession of these looted assets in order to return them to their rightful owners, the Swiss proved to be evasive, uncooperative and outrightly stubborn when it came to giving anything back.

"In essence, according to our own documents, they went out of their way to deceive U.S. negotiators as to how much they retained in Nazi assets, looted or otherwise. In light of this, after more than 50 years, the Swiss must make amends and come clean."

D'Amato added in his letter to Christopher, "I would ask you seek discussions with the Swiss on reopening these negotiations and provide for a proper accounting. .... Clearly the Swiss owe the Allies more than they have admitted to, yet they have managed to escape criticism for this deception for more than 50 years."

The Swiss government last week promised to pay more than $800,000 to two Holocaust groups in a gesture sought by Jewish groups after Switzerland apologised last year for turning back refugees from Nazi terror.

At least two tonnes s of gold looted by the Nazis remains stored in the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank and another four tonnes s in the Bank of England in London from the 1946 agreement. WJC President Edgar Bronfman has asked that this gold be made available to Holocaust survivors and other victims of Nazi persecutions.
A tonne of gold is worth about $10.2 million.
